questions.q: Put these stages in the order they happen when a compiled program is written and then used by a customer.
steps: The programmer writes the source code in an editor
The compiler translates the whole program and reports any errors
The compiler produces an executable file
The executable file is sent to the customer
The customer runs the executable without a translator installed
questions.feedback: Translation happens once, before distribution. That is exactly why the customer needs no translator.

questions.q: A charity needs a program that will run on several makes of computer, be changed by volunteers over many years, and be given out as a file people can simply run. Discuss what language level and what translator you would recommend, and why.

markPoints.concept: a high-level language, because the source can be translated for different machines
markPoints.exemplar: A high-level language, because the same source can be translated for each different make of computer.

markPoints.concept: and because volunteers can read and change high-level code
markPoints.exemplar: Volunteers can also read and change high-level code, which matters over many years.

markPoints.concept: a compiler, because the charity wants to hand out a file people can run
accept: file|executable|hand out|give out|distribut|send|run it|without a translator|on its own
markPoints.exemplar: A compiler, because the charity wants to give out a file people can simply run.

markPoints.concept: the compiled program also runs faster than an interpreted one
markPoints.exemplar: A compiled program also runs faster than the same program being interpreted.

markPoints.concept: but it has to be compiled separately for each kind of machine
markPoints.exemplar: The drawback is that it has to be compiled separately for each kind of machine.

markPoints.concept: and an interpreter would have suited the volunteers' own testing
markPoints.exemplar: An interpreter would still be useful to the volunteers while they are writing and testing changes.

questions.example:
I would recommend a high-level language such as Python or Java. The same source code can be translated for each make of computer, so the charity does not need a separate program for every machine, and high-level code is readable enough that volunteers arriving years later can understand and change it — which would be close to impossible in assembly language.

For the version handed out I would use a compiler. Compiling produces an executable file that people can simply run, with no source code and no translator needed on their computer, and it runs faster than the same program being translated line by line. The drawback is that the program has to be compiled separately for each kind of machine the charity supports, and anyone wanting to change it needs the source and a compiler.

While the volunteers are actually writing the code, an interpreter is the better tool: they can run a half-finished change immediately and see the first error rather than waiting for a full compilation. So the honest answer is both — interpreted while developing, compiled for release.
questions.feedback: Six ideas are available and a good answer reaches a recommendation rather than listing features. Mark yourself on whether you said why each choice suits THIS charity.
questions.hint: Three requirements are given: several makes of computer, years of volunteers, and a file people can run. Take each in turn.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes a compiler or an interpreter.
items: Translates the program once before it runs
Translates each line again every time it is reached
Must be installed on any computer that runs the program
Reports all the errors it found together
Stops at the first error it reaches
questions.feedback: Once versus every time. Every other difference follows from that one.

questions.q: State what is meant by source code.

markPoints.concept: the program as the programmer wrote it, before translation
markPoints.exemplar: The program as the programmer wrote it, before it is translated.

questions.example: The program in the language the programmer wrote it in, before a translator has converted it into machine code.
questions.paraphrase: The original human-readable version of a program, as typed by the programmer and not yet converted.
questions.feedback: What the programmer typed. Machine code is the output of translation, not the source.
